title: Young classical guitarist with progressive right-hand dystonia and new gait change

provenance.citation: Synthetic case drafted 2026-10-17 for Rare Disease Detective. Modeled on typical adult-onset presentations described in the movement-disorder literature; not derived from any individual patient.

demographics.occupation: Classical guitar performance student (conservatory, final year); practices 5–6 hours/day

chief_complaint: "My right-hand fingers curl into my palm when I play, and now it happens when I write too. Lately my right foot turns in when I walk home from rehearsal."
history_of_present_illness: Two years ago the patient noticed that the right middle and ring fingers would curl toward the palm during fast right-hand passages (tremolo and arpeggio), but only after about an hour of practice. Early in a session, playing was normal. Over the following year the curling began earlier in practice sessions and became harder to suppress. She reorganized her schedule to do technical work in the morning because "my hands are just better before lunch"; evening ensemble rehearsals are now the most difficult. About 12 months ago handwriting became effortful, with cramping and excessive grip after roughly half a page. About 5 months ago her roommate noticed her right foot turning inward when they walked home after evening rehearsals; the patient had not noticed it herself. She reports that a nap in the afternoon "sometimes resets" her hand for a short while, which she attributes to reduced fatigue. No pain at rest. No sudden onset, no precipitating injury, no episodes of complete normality interrupted by attacks. No tremor at rest noticed. No speech, swallowing, or cognitive complaints. Mood: frustrated and anxious about her career; no prior psychiatric history.

symptom_timeline.event: Right digits 3–4 curl during fast right-hand passages, only after ~60 min of playing
Seen by hand surgeon; nerve conduction studies normal; referred to neurology
General neurologist diagnoses musician's focal dystonia; recommends retraining and botulinum toxin
Handwriting becomes effortful with cramping after ~half a page
Trihexyphenidyl started; partial benefit; stopped after 6 weeks due to dry mouth and 'foggy' concentration
Two rounds of botulinum toxin to right flexor digitorum superficialis; modest benefit for ~6 weeks each time
Roommate notices right foot inversion when walking home after evening rehearsals
Referred to movement-disorder clinic for second opinion before final-year recital

movement_findings.observation: Involuntary flexion of right digits 3 and 4 at the MCP and PIP joints during right-hand tremolo; appears after ~4 minutes of continuous playing in clinic and progressively worsens.
Compensatory wrist extension and elevation of the right forearm during playing, consistent with an attempt to counteract finger flexion.
Writing: excessive grip on the pen, flexion of digits 3–4, and ulnar deviation of the wrist emerging after ~6 lines; letters become small and cramped.
Mirror movements: mild flexion of right digits 3–4 when the left hand performs rapid finger sequences.
Gait: after ~15 minutes on a treadmill, intermittent right foot inversion with plantar flexion during swing phase; absent at the start of the walk. Running not tested.
At rest and with sustained posture of both arms: no tremor, no dystonic posturing.
Sensory trick: resting the right thumb lightly against the guitar soundboard partially reduces digit flexion.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented, fluent speech, normal attention and recall on bedside testing
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal, including saccades and pursuit; no Kayser–Fleischer rings visible on bedside inspection (no slit lamp performed)
neurological_exam.tone: Normal at rest in all limbs; no rigidity with activation maneuvers
neurological_exam.reflexes: Upper limbs 2+ symmetric. Knees 3+ bilaterally, ankles 2+, no sustained clonus. Right plantar response equivocal; left flexor.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger–nose and heel–shin normal; no dysmetria
neurological_exam.gait: Normal at onset of walking with normal arm swing; see mf_05 for findings after prolonged walking
neurological_exam.bradykinesia_screen: Finger tapping, hand opening, and toe tapping: normal speed and amplitude, no decrement, both sides
neurological_exam.other: Sensation normal. No fasciculations. No postural instability on pull test. Examination performed in late morning.

labs.test: Comprehensive metabolic panel incl. liver enzymes

labs.note: 24-hour urine copper and slit-lamp exam not performed

imaging.modality: MRI brain with and without contrast (3T)
imaging.report: No structural abnormality. Basal ganglia normal in signal and volume. No abnormal susceptibility. No enhancement. Impression: normal MRI brain.
Normal. No cord signal change or foraminal stenosis.

neurophysiology.study: Nerve conduction studies, right upper limb
neurophysiology.report: Normal median, ulnar, and radial motor and sensory conduction. No evidence of entrapment neuropathy.

prior_trials.response: Partial improvement in playing; stopped for dry mouth and impaired concentration

prior_trials.drug: Botulinum toxin A to right FDS (digits 3–4 fascicles)
prior_trials.response: Modest benefit lasting ~6 weeks; mild weakness of finger flexion after the second session

family_history: Father (52) healthy. Mother (50) healthy. One younger brother (19) healthy. Paternal aunt reportedly 'walked on her toes and tripped a lot' as a girl and was told she would 'grow out of it'; she is now in her 50s and walks normally, per the patient. Paternal grandmother had 'shaky hands' in her 70s. No known diagnoses of dystonia, Parkinson disease, or liver disease. No consanguinity.
social_history: Non-smoker. Alcohol: occasional, does not notice effect on symptoms. No recreational drugs. No antipsychotic or antiemetic exposure.
prior_workup_and_opinions: Hand surgeon: no peripheral nerve or tendon cause. General neurologist (~15 months ago): 'Task-specific focal dystonia of the right hand (musician's dystonia). Consider sensorimotor retraining.' The gait change had not yet occurred at that visit.
